palette-generator.quickAnswer: A palette generator builds color schemes from one base color using hue-wheel math. From #4A90D9 (hue 211), the complementary scheme adds hue 211 + 180 = 31, giving #D9944A - a warm amber that sits opposite the blue. Analogous schemes take neighbors at plus/minus 15-30 degrees for calm designs; triadic and tetradic schemes use evenly spaced hues for energy.
keyFacts: Complementary = base hue + 180 degrees: maximum hue contrast, two colors.
Analogous = base hue plus/minus 15-30 degrees: calm, nature-like harmony.
Triadic = three hues 120 degrees apart: balanced but vibrant.
Tetradic = two complementary pairs (rectangle on the wheel): rich, needs careful balance.
Split-complementary = base plus the two neighbors of its complement: strong contrast, easier than full complementary.
Saturation and lightness stay at the base color's values, so every scheme feels related.
howTo: Enter your base color with the picker or a HEX code like #4A90D9.
Pick a scheme: complementary, analogous, triadic, tetradic, split-complementary or monochromatic.
The palette appears instantly as swatches with HEX codes.
Tap any swatch to copy its HEX.
Use the base color for 60% of the design, the scheme colors for 30% and 10%.
palette-generator.formula:
Each scheme color = HSL(base hue + offset, base saturation, base lightness).
Example: #4A90D9 -> HSL(211, 65%, 57%).
Complementary: offset +180 -> HSL(31, 65%, 57%) = RGB(217, 148, 74) = #D9944A.
Analogous: offsets -30, -15, +15, +30 around hue 211.
palette-generator.workedExample:
Base #4A90D9 = HSL(211, 65%, 57%), complementary scheme:
1. Add 180 to the hue: 211 + 180 = 391, wrapped to 31 degrees.
2. Keep saturation 65% and lightness 57%.
3. HSL(31, 65%, 57%) converts to RGB(217, 148, 74).
4. In HEX: 217 = D9, 148 = 94, 74 = 4A -> #D9944A.
5. Result: deep blue #4A90D9 paired with warm amber #D9944A - classic opposite-wheel harmony.
benefits: Six professional schemes from a single brand color in seconds.
Every scheme is mathematically harmonious - no clashing by construction.
Copy-ready HEX codes drop straight into CSS or design tools.
Great for logos, websites and presentations that need a full palette fast.
limitations: Math harmony is a starting point - always judge the palette with your eyes.
Tetradic schemes have four strong colors; use one as dominant or the design feels chaotic.
Scheme colors may still fail WCAG text contrast - check pairs you use for text.

faqs.q: Which scheme should I choose for a website?
faqs.a: Start with analogous for calm, content-heavy sites, or complementary when you need one strong accent (like a call-to-action button). Triadic suits playful brands; tetradic is for rich, complex designs.

faqs.q: Why do scheme colors keep the same saturation and lightness?
faqs.a: Keeping them fixed makes every color feel like it belongs to the same family. If the tool also varied saturation, some schemes would look random rather than designed.
A classic guideline: 60% of the design uses the dominant color, 30% a secondary, 10% an accent. It keeps even bold palettes feeling balanced.

faqs.q: Can a palette have more than these schemes?
faqs.a: The six schemes here cover the standard color-theory set used in professional design. Combining schemes (e.g. analogous base + complementary accent) is how designers extend them.

faqs.q: Do these schemes work for dark mode?
faqs.a: The hue relationships work in any mode. For dark mode, take the same hues and lower the lightness of backgrounds while keeping accents bright.
Yes - every HEX is computed from the HSL math and rounded to the nearest whole RGB value, then shown exactly as computed.
